lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.quote: In *sumulat* from *sulat*, *-um-* helps form a verb in which the doer carries out the action. In *Sumulat siya ng liham*, the word means that the person wrote a letter.

lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.quote: A **root** or **base** is the main meaningful part of a word. An **affix** is a word part added to a base to change its meaning or job in a sentence.
lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.note: The former lexical/bound-form wording has been replaced by short, concrete definitions that are substantially simpler.

lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.quote: Do not split every word that begins with the same letters. A word part is useful only when it truly belongs to the word and helps explain its meaning.
lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.note: The dense “mechanically productive” and “transparent root” language has been replaced by short plain-English guidance.

lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.quote: For example, *un-* works as a prefix in *unhappy* because *happy* is a meaningful base and *un-* changes it to the opposite idea. Do not split *uncle* into *un-* and *cle*. The letters *un* are there, but *cle* is not the meaningful base of the word.

lesson-vocabulary-root-words-prefixes-su.quote: Word structure is the way meaningful parts are joined in a word. A word's origin is where it came from in an older language or earlier form. These clues can help, but letters that only look familiar are not enough.
